Spanish/Portuguese Support

Spanish/Portuguese Support (incidents)
(Knowledge index)
INDEX
WHAT
WHY
WHEN
HOW
Steps
Identify a user’s preferred language
Incident handling
English Speaking Specialists
Bilingual Specialists
Details
Non-English intake and agreement forms
Update user’s preferred language
Unsupported languages
Emails
Related
What
(return to index)
The Spanish and Portuguese team supports Thumbtack users who need other language support to effectively communicate their version of what happened in their incidents and to properly understand the steps they need to take to resolve them. This helps Thumbtack drive impact and support our user base. 

Why
(return to index)
Thumbtack values our diverse user base. To provide an equitable experience for all users, we provide them the opportunity to communicate via phone and email in their preferred language with T&S specialists who can also communicate proficiently in that language.
When
(return to index)
Incidents in which either user requests Spanish or Portuguese support should be flagged and sent to the Spanish and Portuguese team for handling.
T&S Specialists should use the Spanish forms when dealing with Thumbtack Trust & Safety Agreements and Intake Documentation for MBG / PDG / CSAT.
How
(return to index)
   Steps 
      (return to index)

IDENTIFY A USER’S PREFERRED LANGUAGE
(return to index)
In Tack, there are 2 ways you can identify a user’s preferred language:
User flags:
From the incident, go to the Customer or Pro tabs and look for a Spanish Support or Portuguese Support flag under the Customer Success Guidance section.
[Image: rtaImage]
From a case or Work Ticket (WT), go to the Thumbtack User section and look for a Spanish Support or Portuguese Support flag.
[Image: rtaImage]
The Preferred Language field on the user’s Contact:
If this field is blank, we assume English is their preferred language.
[Image: rtaImage]
INCIDENT OVERVIEW
(return to index)
English speaking specialists
In some cases, a user may not have noted their language preference before an incident is created. Since these accounts don’t have a user flag or preferred language in our system at the time of categorization, these incidents go to the general queue.
If you come across an incident with a user who requests Spanish or Portuguese language support, follow the steps below:

Update the user’s preferred language
If you haven’t made any contact with either user, move on to step 3. If you’ve already been in contact with either user, follow the steps below:
Notate the incident using \Spanish queue
Follow up with the user requesting other language support
If Spanish is preferred, send \Spanish transfer
If Portuguese is preferred, send \Portuguese transfer
Note: Both snippets translate to “Thank you for letting us know you would prefer assistance in [Spanish/Portuguese]. I am happy to send this case to a specialist who can assist you in your preferred language. A [Spanish/Portuguese] speaking specialist will be reaching out to you shortly. Please allow 3-5 business days as I transfer the case.
If the other user is English preferred, follow up with them using \engspanishneed.
If you have a pending call scheduled with either user, tag @mtsspanish in the #ts-incidentops-casediscussion Slack channel to coordinate a more timely follow-up.
Reassign the incident to a queue and select "MTS Spanish."
Bilingual Specialists
All incidents that require Spanish or Portuguese language support will go to the MTS-Spanish queue for Omni assignment.

Review the incident.
If the incident has previously been worked on and was transferred, follow these steps:
Review the incident and any specialist notes
Be sure to note any previously scheduled calls to ensure appointments are met or rescheduled.
If the incident is new, complete the initial incident review.
Contact the user requesting Spanish or Portuguese support in their preferred language.
If the user responds in English or states they prefer English, move forward in English.
Let them know you’ll update their account’s language preference, remove the user’s preferred language flag, and update the Preferred Language on their Contact.
Move forward with the determined incident handling approach.
As needed throughout your incident, reference Thumbtack’s official Spanish Common Terms to ensure consistency across all teams.
   Details
      (return to index)
NON-ENGLISH INTAKE AND AGREEMENT FORMS
When possible, Specialists should send documentation, intake, and agreement forms in the user's preferred language. This option will populate when sending a form in Ironclad. The following forms are currently available:
Thumbtack Guarantee Submission Form (Spanish)
Thumbtack Payment Agreement (Spanish)
Thumbtack Reimbursement Agreement (Spanish)
Wire Transfer Request Form (Spanish)
For more information, refer to the “Sending through Incident” section of the Navigate Ironclad KA.
UPDATE USER’S PREFERRED LANGUAGE
    (return to index)
To update the user’s preferred language, follow the steps below:

Add a user flag in Tack.
For Name, enter “Spanish Support” or “Portuguese Support” based on their preferred language.
For Flag Type, select the corresponding preferred language support flag.
Click Save.
[Image: rtaImage]
Update the Preferred Language on the user’s contact.
Click the user’s name from the corresponding incident tab.
Under Contact Preferences, click the pencil icon next to Preferred Language.
[Image: rtaImage]
Select their preferred language from the dropdown.
Click Save.
UNSUPPORTED LANGUAGES
(return to index)
Currently, we only offer T&S support in English, Spanish, and Portuguese. If a user requests support in any other language, we aren’t able to accommodate them at this time. Submit a feedback report regarding the language the user is requesting, so these requests can be tracked.
If translation services are needed, you can encourage them to find a family member, friend, or neighbor to assist them.
   Emails
    (return to index)
SPANISH EMAIL TRANSLATIONS

Spanish Macros
GRAMMARLY SNIPPETS
\Spanish transfer: Send this Grammarly snippet to let users know that the case is being transferred to the Spanish team for further assistance.
\Portuguese transfer: Send this Grammarly snippet to let users know that the case is being transferred to a Portuguese-speaking specialist for further assistance.
\Spanish transfer (English): Use this Grammarly snippet to let English-speaking users on the incident know that the incident is being transferred to ensure the 
\Spanish queue: Use this Grammarly snippet to note the incident before transferring it to the Spanish queue.

What 
​​(return to index) 
The Social Media team monitors and responds to interactions across platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and TikTok, as well as selected other sites. This includes comments, replies, tags, shares, direct messages, and external reviews, ensuring a consistent and proactive approach to engagement across all relevant channels. 
Why 
​​(return to index) 
Users may share feedback, ask questions, and raise concerns on social media platforms. By actively monitoring and responding across platforms, we can provide timely support, foster trust, and protect and strengthen Thumbtack’s brand.
When

All interactions or engagement on Thumbtack’s social media are managed through our moderation tool, Hootsuite, with additional review sites requiring direct monitoring. Our team focuses on addressing potential T&S issues, engaging with user questions, concerns, and feedback to foster a supportive and responsive online presence. 
SLA for social media moderation is 24 hours, and Target HT is 3 minutes.

When to use
Steps
Respond

    (return to index)

BRAND VOICE
​​(return to index) 
In our public-facing communication, Specialists should stick to the Thumbtack brand voice, which aims to come across as relatable, grounded, and natural. While assisting customers and pros on social media, tone should focus on being helpful, instructive, and supportive.


PHRASES TO AVOID
PHRASES TO INCORPORATE
Overused sympathy
Don’t start every message saying, “We apologize for the inconvenience.” 
Jargon (TT internal terms)
We dug around and…
Let’s take a look
Let’s check this out
We checked it out
Glad you’re reaching out
We hear you
Thanks for letting us know.
That’s not the experience we want.
We want to help.
We’re listening
QUALITY & TONE GUIDELINES
​​(return to index) 
Best Practices for Responding
Respond Promptly:
Aim to respond to new reviews within 24-48 hours, especially for negative feedback. This shows attentiveness and dedication.
Be Professional and Empathetic:
Maintain a calm and courteous tone, even if the review is negative or unfair.
Apologize for any negative experience, even when not agreeing with the customer's full assessment.
Show empathy for their frustration or disappointment.
Avoid defensiveness or making excuses.
Never blame the customer or the Thumbtack pro.
Personalize Your Response:
Avoid canned responses. Tailor each reply to the specific points raised in the review.
Address the customer by name if available.
Mention specific details from their review to show you've read it carefully.
Acknowledge the Issue and Offer Solutions:
Clearly acknowledge the problem or concern mentioned. Confirm details and avoid making assumptions
Focus on finding a resolution. If a solution isn't immediately available, explain what steps are being taken or the plan to prevent similar issues. Let the customer know Thumbtack is committed to finding a resolution.
If appropriate, offer to take the conversation offline (e.g., provide an email address or phone number) to resolve complex or sensitive matters privately.
Thank Customers for Their Feedback:
Always express gratitude for both positive (i.e., 4-5 star ratings) and negative reviews. This shows you value their input.
Show appreciation for them taking the time to raise the issue.
Learn and Improve:
Identify recurring themes or issues in reviews. Use this feedback to identify areas for internal improvement in products, services, or processes.
When applicable, mention any changes or improvements made based on customer feedback.
Maintain Company Brand Voice:
Ensure all responses align with Thumbtack’s established brand voice.
When it makes sense, highlight Thumbtack's core values and reliability to rebuild trust.
Positive Reviews:
While negative reviews take priority, briefly acknowledge and thank customers for positive feedback, especially if they offer helpful suggestions or express extreme gratitude. Avoid generic "thank yous" for every 5-star review, as it can clutter the page.
ESCALATE TO A MANAGER
​​(return to index) 
For serious issues, typically involving brand risk or Critical Escalations issues, loop in your manager. After their review, follow the usual process for contacting or notifying the Critical Escalations team, then create a quick case with all the available details.

What

Review dispute moderation is the process of handling disputes submitted by pros who have concerns about a Thumbtack review left by a customer on Thumbtack. The goal is to determine whether the review should be removed, left as is, or escalated, in accordance with Thumbtack's Terms of Use.
The following concerns are subject to review dispute moderation:
Reviews that are not based on a verified interaction or are posted outside of the allowed timeframe.
Reviews that the pro is concerned were incentivized, duplicated, fake, fraudulent, or misleading.
Reviews (including any attached images) containing profanity, discrimination, personal information (PII), or harassment.
Reviews that violate privacy or constitute commercial promotion.
Reviews that should have been verified, but were missed by the automated system. 

Why
Authentic reviews are essential for establishing trust with Thumbtack’s users. The Review dispute moderation process protects Thumbtack by ensuring disputed reviews are reviewed quickly and consistently. This ultimately provides pros with fairness, customers with reliable information, and Thumbtack with lasting credibility.
When 
The process is triggered when a pro disputes a customer review through a frontline team (Service & Support, Sales, Partnerships, or Trust & Safety). The frontline agent creates a case, completes the "Review Dispute" section, and transfers it to the Proactive MI Queue using the Salesforce transfer flow. A specialist then reviews the evidence, makes a final decision, and notifies the pro of the outcome via email.
SLA for this queue is 72 hours with a handling time (HT) target of 15 minutes per case.

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS
This process primarily deals with customer-initiated reviews that a pro is disputing as a policy violation. We only remove reviews that violate the Content and Review Policy & Non-Discrimination Policy.
How
   Steps

GUIDING PRINCIPLES
Here are a few things to keep in mind while working this queue. 
Thumbtack’s stance is not to remove reviews unless a clear violation of the Content and Review Policy is confirmed.
Edits are Prohibited. Specialists are limited to either removing the review or leaving it. We do not edit reviews.
Thumbtack is neutral. If the customer and pro interacted, we will not arbitrate what happened or did not happen or the veracity of the review.
If a lead is refunded, it does not automatically disqualify a review. Reviews are judged solely on the interaction between the customer and the pro.
PROCESS FLOW CHART

Review Dispute Moderation

[Image: rtaImage]

PROCESS OVERVIEW

[Image: rtaImage]
 
[Image: rtaImage]
Open the Case (auto-assigned through Omni).
On the right side, click the Related tab and scroll down to Support Processes.
Click on the open Review Dispute link under the Record Name to open up the Support Process.
Check the indicated Dispute Reason, Review Link, General Comments and any files left by the agent to understand what the dispute request is about.
Pull up the Review Link in Admin and check the following in the review thread to assess the customer and pro interaction history.
Text 
Pro name 
Customer name 
Request/Projects
Quote/Negotiations
Go to the customer’s page in Admin and check Linked Users for clear signs of competitors' contact abuse or deceptive practices
If yes, action the account in line with our Terms of Service. 
If the review is confirmed to contain high-severity content (Discrimination, Critical Escalation), escalate the dispute to the appropriate team.
Determine if the review will be removed based on the Content and Review Policy, the Removal & Actioning Table and record the decision:
If a violation is found, Removed Review.
If no violation is found, Leave Review #CBB.
If additional information is required, email the pro/cx to request the information before making a final decision.
Note: For cases requiring additional information, change the case status to “Pending Customer” while waiting for the pro/cx to respond.
Go back to the record in the Support Process, fill out details on the right-hand side and select the applicable Manager Decision.
For reviews with no violation found, a manager comment should be left stating:
“The review has been investigated and found not to violate our Content and Review Policy; based on the evidence available within the dispute, this decision is final."
Email the pro directly using the appropriate email address and template from the Email Templates and close the Case.
   Details
     

REVIEW REMOVAL AND ACTIONING TABLE



VIOLATION
ADMIN ACTIONING

SALESFORCE  ACTIONING

VIOLATION
ADMIN ACTION
INTERNAL NOTES
MANAGER DECISION
MANAGER COMMENTS
The review is not based on an actual or attempted interaction between the pro and customer (i.e., no contact, communication or engagement of any kind).
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (No Interaction)
Removed Review
The review has been removed because the customer and pro did not have a confirmed interaction, which violates our Content and Review Policy.
The review was posted >6 months after the last interaction or >1 year after the final day of the project end.
Exception: Long-lead projects (e.g., attorney, home builds) require proof of work.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (exceeded allowable time limit)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as it was posted outside of the allowable time limit set by our Content and Review Policy.
The review is gibberish, a single punctuation mark or something of the sort.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Unrelated Content)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as the content was unrelated to the service experience and violated our Content Policy.
The review content is unrelated to the pro’s conduct, professionalism, or job experience.
E.g., political commentary, content about a third party.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Unrelated Content)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as the content was unrelated to the service experience and violated our Content Policy.
The review text or case details strongly indicate it was intended for a different pro.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Wrong Pro)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as it was found to be intended for a different professional
The review text is an exact duplicate of another review for the pro by the same customer. Including those imported from another platform.
Delete the latest duplicate Review or verified TT Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Duplicate)
Removed Review
The newer review has been removed as it was a duplicate of a previously submitted review.
The review text contains PII (full names, email, phone numbers, URLs, social media handles).
Exception: Pro's first and last name is permitted, if visible on profile.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (PII present)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as it violates privacy standards (PII)
The review contains images displaying PII or unauthorized content, such as photos of individuals (like minors), billing statements or private documents of Pro/Cx.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (PII present or Minor Individual)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as it violates privacy standards (PII)
Content that promotes another business or service is included.
E.g., "I went with Company X instead" or "Check out my new website..."
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Commercial Promotion)
Removed Review
The review has been removed because it violated our policy regarding commercial promotion.
Pro/Cx requested removal within 24 hours* due to a typo, redundant text, misleading TT email or mismatched rating. The review will only be removed if it has an identical duplicate.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (24hr Exception)
Removed Review
The review has been removed as a courtesy regarding the error duplicate due to [INSERT REASON]
The review contains suspiciously fake or AI-Generated Images.
Delete Review
Review Dispute - Removed (Misleading/Fake content via AI)
Removed Review
The review has been removed for containing fake or AI-generated images, which are misleading and violate our Content and Review Policy.
NOTE:*The 24-hour exception is a narrow service courtesy only. It is NOT a general policy or a loophole for removing substantive reviews. 
SCENARIOS FOR ESCALATIONS



SCENARIOS
ACTION
Discrimination Accusations: The review contains language that is vulgar, obscene, threatening, possibly be discriminatory, or profane when directed at the other party.
Leave a comment identifying this as a discrimination case and transfer to Marketplace Integrity, which will escalate to the NDP Team.
Critical Content/Photos (Images): The review includes inappropriate images, child safety violations or highly sensitive content (violence, illegal activity, etc.)
Immediately stop processing and follow the critical escalation process. Reach out directly to the Critical Escalations team via Slack in #escalation_questions.
Legal Settlements/Court Cases: If the pro requests to remove a review due to a claim of an ongoing legal case or explicitly threatens legal action.
Removal is considered only if the pro provides valid, formal legal documentation explicitly requesting Thumbtack to remove it. If documentation is received, immediately stop processing and follow the critical escalation process to escalate.
Suspected Systemic Fraud: If, during dispute review, evidence of systemic fraud (e.g., LADs + IP Match, or multiple Fake Reviews KA criteria, extortion) or possible "Spammy/Fake" customer lead reviews are found.
The case should be escalated to SME’s handling #anomaly_detection_global. This escalation is required to ensure the entire network is investigated and account-level penalties (suspension/removal) are properly enforced

REVIEW VERIFICATION

Occasionally, a Thumbtack customer will review a pro, but the review will not show as verified on their profile. If the review should have been verified, pros can contact the support team to fix it.
To verify a review, proactive specialists should follow the steps below:
The support agent should have provided the Review PKID, as well as the customer and pro PKIDs or admin links and the Project bid. If not, follow the steps below to:
Open the Review in admin.
Click the pro and customer names to open their user admin pages.
In the customer admin, scroll down and expand the Project section.
Select the project that matches the review. Make sure the category and pro are correct.
Confirm that the customer & pro Names, PKID and Bid PKIDs match exactly across the Review, Project Bid and Admin profile; and that the review was left within the last 30 days.
If the above conditions are all confirmed, go to the top Review action list on the right-hand side of the review page and click add bid to review.
[Image: rtaImage]
In the next window, enter the Bid ID.
In the box under “ Why you wants to associate this review with this bid?” enter "verification" or "verifying review."
[Image: rtaImage]
Click Convert Review

SUSPICIOUSLY FAKE OR AI-GENERATED IMAGES

Customers using fake or AI-generated images in reviews damages a Pro's reputation, violates our policies and destroys the trust users have in our marketplace. Below are steps to take to confirm if a photo is suspiciously fake or AI-generated.
Always visually inspect images for unnatural textures, anatomical errors, or logical inconsistencies.
Check File Names and Look for keywords like "gemini," "chatgpt," "grok," or "dall-e." Users often neglect to rename AI-generated files. Do not change the labels of these photos as they are evidence.
Verify Metadata by downloading the image to check its digital history.
Mac: Right-click → Get Info → More Info.
Windows: Right-click → Properties → Details.
Red Flags: Look for AI software labels or URLs (e.g., "chatgpt.com", “edited by with Google AI”, “Adobe fire-fly” ) or a total lack of camera hardware data.
Technical Tools: Use Gemini to check for SynthID watermarks or Chat GPT for C2PA metadata. If the tool confirms the image is AI-generated, it is a violation.
Note: Screenshots strip metadata and credentials, allowing users to bypass these technical checks.
Decision Guidance: If technical evidence is missing but the investigation strongly suggests the image is fake, trust your instincts and judgment when making a decision.

TIER GUIDE
(return to index)
In reviewing Pro accounts, you may encounter some of the following TOS violations.

TIER
WHAT THAT MEANS
TYPES OF TOS VIOLATIONS
Tier 4-6
Violations that can't be fixed and the pro must not only be removed from the platform but require further attention from the Critical Escalations team.

Refer to the Escalation Process for steps.

Self- Assassination
Mercenary Services
Child Pornography
Tier 3
Violations that can't be 'fixed' and the pro needs to be removed from the platform. The core service that the pro offers is either sexual, illegal, malicious or just generally something we'd never want on our platform.
Sexual Content
Legally Questionable

Inappropriate Content/ Language (Profanity or explicit language that expresses hate, or is directed to a person, group, organization, etc.)
Discrimination

Tier 2
Violations that can't be 'fixed', but the pro doesn't need to be deleted/blocklisted because the profile wasn't so risky. The core service, or parts of the way it is offered, are not allowed on the platform, and a new Service Profile needs to be created.
Inappropriate Content/ Language (Profanity or explicit language that serves as an expression and Inappropriate profile photos or uploaded photos)
Mismatched Category
Not A Thumbtack Service
Not A Service
Non-US Service Location
Tier 1

What
(return to index)
The T&S Proactive MI Queue handles T&S cases from front-facing teams. These cases require thorough analysis and investigation to identify risks, implement resolutions and communicate any final decisions directly to users.

Why
(return to index)
These are Trust and Safety Issues that frontline support shouldn’t handle. They often need a deeper look to ensure potential ToS violations have been addressed. This queue also triages cases that need further analysis by T&S Risk Analysts.

When
(return to index)
A case is forwarded to the Proactive MI Queue when it falls under any of the following issue types:
Linked Accounts
Inaccurately Ghosted Accounts
Non-US IP Reports
Fake Reviews
Contact Avoidance
Scam / Fraud Reports
Account Takeover (ATO) & Identity Theft
Review Dispute Moderation
Concern About a User
SLA for this queue is 72 hours, and AHT varies greatly, depending on the severity of the case.
How
(return to index)
After taking over a case, proactive ops specialists investigate and communicate the final decision directly to the user before closing the case. Cases should not be transferred back to Service.

   Steps
    (return to index)

PROCESS OVERVIEW
(return to index)
After receiving the case, scroll down to the Most Recent Activity and read through the MTS Transfer details to get a summary of the issue.
Using the PKID provided in the summary, search Admin and investigate the case based on the scenario identified in the proactive case guide below. 
Once the investigation is complete and all necessary steps are taken, compile your findings and results. 
Document this information as a "Post" on the case to notify others of the actions taken, and also record it as an Admin comment along with the relevant case number.
Email the user directly using the appropriate template from the Email section:
Make sure to update the Sender field with the correct email address for the email being sent.
Close the case using the following settings. Do NOT transfer back to Service:
Category: Marketplace Integrity
Sub Category: Other

Status: Closed

Ready-to-send email templates are available for every scenario in the case guide. Templates are organized by category and clearly marked with the correct sending address. When sending emails, the following guidelines should be followed:
Always update the “from” email field for the specific email being sent.
Use do-not-reply@thumbtack.com (DNR) for notifying the pro of the final decisions from T&S. If any reply comes in, it is routed to Service as a new case.
Use trustandsafetyteam@thumbtack.com (TTS) when requesting documents or additional information from the pro/customer. Allows the user to reply directly to the Proactive MI Queue.
Always use the approved process emails within Salesforce.
Follow the steps to email and insert a template outlined in the Salesforce: Case Navigation and Management (Rep) Support KA.Use the “all classic templates” folder when searching for email templates.
Always fill in all highlighted placeholders before sending. Highlighted text is usually bracketed and bolded in red.
Ex: [INSERT REASON FROM MANAGER COMMENTS]
Ensure to follow the language standards from the email guide.

articles.fullText:
Pro reports

Pro Reports
(Knowledge index)
INDEX
WHAT
WHY
WHEN
HOW
Steps
Pro not paid
In-product reports
Pro self-reports
Details
Pro doesn’t want us to contact the customer
Pro never responds or becomes unresponsive
Filling out the Eligibility Review
Refunding the pro
Pro’s local resources
Talking points
Emails
What
(return to index)
Pro reports are incidents where the pro is reporting another user for a T&S issue. This can include not being paid (or only paid partially) after doing work for a Thumbtack customer, reporting a customer for behavior or safety concerns, or other potential ToS violations.
Pros can also use Thumbtack as a customer. However, any project concerns reported by a pro using the platform as a customer should be worked using the standard mediation process. 
Why
(return to index)
Trust and Safety’s mission is to make sure all users are having safe, abuse-free, and positive experiences on Thumbtack. Any pro reports should be worked with this in mind. 
When
(return to index)
Primarily, pro reports come through the in-product report (IPR) flow. However, pros occasionally reach out through other reporting methods as well. Pro concerns may come up on project-related issues or customer reports as well.  
How
(return to index)
   Steps
   (return to index)
PRO NOT PAID
(return to index)
Process Overview 
Complete your initial review. Confirm we know:
Amount owed, contract, actions already taken, invoices, etc.
Do we already have enough info to move forward?
No - Call the pro or send the PNP: Gather info - pro template.
Yes - Call the pro or send the PNP: Explain process - pro macro.
Let the pro know we’ll contact the customer about the situation.
Send the macro PNP: First email - cx to customer to the customer and wait 2 business days for a response.
Review the customer’s response:
Customer is willing to pay
Establish a timeline to confirm an agreement is made.
Follow the usual incident mediation steps to help the users fulfill their agreement.
The customer has concerns with the project:
Move forward as a normal project concern incident, and decide what methods/tools/processes you'll use to assist the users.
If the customer doesn’t want our assistance, follow the usual steps when a customer withdraws their dispute.
Customer is unresponsive or is unwilling to pay:
If unresponsive, call the customer. (if a phone number is available.)
Unlike the usual expectation for unresponsive users, customers in PNP scenarios don’t need the same number of contacts. 1 email and a call (if possible) will suffice.
If they’re still unresponsive or unwilling, remove and blocklist the customer’s account.
If they’re a customer member, follow the steps to cancel their “auto-renew.”
Refund the customer lead to the pro’s Thumbtack balance.
Notify the pro that we’ve removed the customer, refunded the lead, and encourage them to look into their local resources.
If the pro responds looking for more help, you can send the PNP: Pro wants more help email.
Update the Guarantee eligibility review.
Close the incident.
IN-PRODUCT REPORTS
(return to index)
In-product reports are submitted through the Thumbtack product so pros can easily report issues or request a refund. When the report includes a T&S concern, it’s sent to the incident handling team for further investigation and follow up.

Process Overview
Review the pro’s comments. Do we already have enough info to review and determine action?
No - Request more information.
If the pro doesn’t respond, follow the usual steps before considering them unresponsive.
Yes - Move to step 2.
If you don’t see details on the incident, click into the attached case to locate the Work Ticket (WT). Here, you’ll see the full comments submitted by the pro.
Investigate the complaint
Does it involve a behavior or safety concern?
Can you confirm what the pro is reporting?
Ex., the pro reports a customer for harassment. We might need additional context on the situation, screenshots of communication, etc.
Is the pro self-reporting?
Did they exhibit unprofessional behavior themselves?
Are they informing us of a project concern when the customer hasn’t reported directly?
Thank the pro for their report and action either account appropriately:
No action
Flag
Coach
Remove
Note: You aren’t required to include your scheduling link in your emails for these reports.  
Pro self-reports 

Sometimes, a pro reports a customer, but after investigating, we find issues with the pro as well. When this is the case, we may need to take action with their account, in addition to potential action on the customer account. This can include:
Coaching for behavior concerns
Unprofessional behavior
Setting expectations
Unresolved project issues when the customer hasn’t reached out to Thumbtack directly.

   Details
   (return to index)
PRO DOESN’T WANT US TO CONTACT CUSTOMER
(return to index)
Similar to customer reports, we can’t offer the pro much help if they won’t allow us to reach out to the customer. When a pro doesn’t want us to reach out to the customer:
Let them know that we’re unable to assist without involving the customer.
For pro-not-paid situations, this includes refunds on the quote - we can’t confirm that the customer didn’t pay if we can’t reach out to them.
Give the pro some information about local resources they can use.
Explain that we’ll close the incident but that we’re happy to help if they change their mind about us reaching out to the customer.
Pro never responds or becomes unresponsive

This applies only to situations where the customer hasn’t expressed concerns with the project.
After two business days, send a reminder email to give the pro time to respond.
If the pro still hasn’t responded in 1-2 business days, cold call the pro.
If they still don’t respond, send them an email letting them know that we’re closing the incident.
Flag the customer’s account for a possible non-payment issue.
Note: If you’ve already reached out to the customer, let them know that we’re closing the incident due to the pro’s lack of response but that we encourage them to follow up with the pro in regards to payment.

FILLING OUT THE ELIGIBILITY REVIEW
(return to index)
Customer is unresponsive or not involved

If the customer has been unresponsive and you’re getting ready to close the incident, the way you fill out the Guarantee Eligibility Review will be a bit different. Since the Guarantee is only for customers, we would still be filling it out for the customer’s eligibility, but our selections will be based on the information we have been provided by the pro. The information may not always be available or accurate, so use the info you do have to fill out all the required fields as best you can.
Customer is responsive
If the customer is responsive, you’ll fill out the Guarantee Eligbility Review as you normally would on any other incident, as outlined through the Guarantee process.
REFUNDING THE PRO
(return to index)
We’ll refund the cost of the lead if the customer is unresponsive or unwilling to pay the pro without reasonable justification.
Although this may be a small gesture, we want the pro to know that we care about their business, experience, and success on Thumbtack. Pros shouldn’t have to pay for the lead on top of the money the customer owes them, so this can lessen the sting and keep the pro engaged on Thumbtack.

When you refund the pro
Categorize the refund in Admin as a "courtesy refund" and note that the refund is for a pro not paid incident and the incident number.
Note in your incident that you've refunded the pro.
Note: If there’s an in-product refund request, you’ll need to refund through the link on the corresponding WT, as well as update the Outcome field before you’re able to close your incident.
PRO’S LOCAL RESOURCES
(return to index)
Pros have several options available to them to pursue customers outside on their own. Some pros may reach out to a local Chamber of Commerce or industry organization to connect with other local businesses for advice, and they can also check their local government for additional assistance.
The best option for most pros will be to continue contacting the customer and requesting payment (in a professional manner) while taking steps to protect themselves in the future. Suggest things like:
Establish a contract to clearly outline the work and terms for payment.
Take reasonable deposits.
Practice good communication throughout a project to address issues as they come up.

Small claims, liens, etc.

Other methods, such as small claims court, liens, etc., can be frustrating for both parties and problematic for Thumbtack. If the pro brings these options up – encourage them to look into whatever options may be best for their business, but we can’t recommend a particular course of action.

Creating a business contract
If it’s not already a part of their business practices, encourage pros to create a contract to help them in the future. Contracts are helpful in clearly defining the work and any terms surrounding payment. This is a good way for pros to protect themselves and their business.
While we are not associated with Rocket Lawyer, we can direct the pro to their free contract generator as a helpful resource to get them started - https://www.rocketlawyer.com/document/business-contract.rl#/
For a more robust or personalized contract, we can encourage the pro to contact an attorney for assistance. Do not direct them to a specific attorney or provide anything that could be construed as legal advice.
    Talking points
   (return to index)
CUSTOMER VOICEMAIL SCRIPT
(return to index)
Hi, this is [name] reaching out from Thumbtack about your recent [request category] project with [pro name/business name]. They contacted us and let us know they had completed the work but hadn’t received payment yet. We wanted to get your perspective on the situation and see how we can help. I’ll be sending you a follow-up email to [customer email], so you can reply to that, or you can schedule a call with me using the link included in the email. Thanks!
TALKING POINTS
(return to index)
I completed the work, but my customer hasn’t paid!
I’m sorry you’re having this experience - I know it can be frustrating to have to contact a customer about paying you, especially when you’ve already done work for them.
I’ll be reaching out to them to get more information and to see how Thumbtack can help. I’ll follow up with you within two business days.
My customer hasn’t paid me and I want to take legal action (filing a lien, etc.)
I understand. As a pro, you have multiple resources to help you and I’d recommend looking into all of the options you have locally. In the meantime, I’m happy to help you contact this customer to see if we can help you get this resolved quickly.
What local resources do I have to collect payment?
Keep this discussion at a high level without directing the pro to specific resources. If possible, pivot to coaching the pro on how to prevent these issues in the future.
I can’t go into much detail because I’m not legally trained to provide guidance in these cases. But other pros in this position may reach out to their local government for information. Or if there’s a local chamber of commerce, you may be able to get advice from other local businesses about how they’ve handled these types of issues.
Why am I being forced into a dispute resolution process?
When we reached out to your customer, they mentioned [issue about the project], and it’s their understanding that the service was not completed as agreed. Because there’s a dispute about the project and what needs to be paid for, we want to help you both come to a solution.
Refunding the contact doesn’t come close to the payment I’m owed!
We’ve removed this customer from Thumbtack until we hear this concern is resolved. This absolutely isn’t the experience we want pros to have and not the type of contact you should be paying for, so we’ve refunded this lead as a courtesy.
We know this doesn’t replace the money you’re owed for the work you’ve done. We’re just trying to help within the limits we have.
Does the Thumbtack Guarantee cover me if the customer didn’t pay me?
The Thumbtack Guarantee only covers eligible customers in the event something is damaged, or their project isn’t completed as outlined and agreed on.
It would not apply to situations like this. I’m happy to help you contact the customer and work out payment, but ultimately they will be responsible for paying you.
I haven’t paid because there are issues with the work (customer).
Thanks for letting me know. I’d like to help you work with [pro] towards a solution. While we expect pros to be paid for their work, we also expect them to address any issues with the project. Let’s talk about how Thumbtack can help the two of you get things resolved.
Can I make a payment through Thumbtack? (customer)
Customers can pay service providers using Thumbtack Pay. Simply select the pro you want to pay from your account’s Inbox tab and click Pay this pro. You can refer to the steps in our Help Center here for additional information
Before sending any payment, I’d encourage you to contact the pro to arrange and agree on your payment method to ensure they can receive it.
   Emails
   (return to index)
EMAIL TEMPLATES
(return to index)
PNP: Gather info - pro: Specialists should use this email macro at the beginning of the incident when they need more info from the pro.
PNP: Explain process—pro: Specialists should send this email macro to the pro when they have enough information to contact the customer about the concerns.
PNP: First email - cx: Specialists should send this email macro to the customer at the beginning of the incident when it’s time to contact the customer.
PNP: Unresponsive - cx: Specialists should send this email tio the customer if the customer is unresponsive to their first email for 2 business days.
PNP: Customer unwilling - pro: Specialists should send this email to the pro if the customer was unresponsive or responded that they won’t pay the pro.
PNP: Intro process - pro: Send to pro if customer let us know about concerns with the project and we’re moving forward with a resolution process.
PNP: Intro process - cx: Send to customer if the customer shares concerns with the project, and we’re moving forward with a resolution process.
PNP: Customer willing - cx: Send this email to customer if they let us know they’re willing to pay.
PNP: Already paid - cx: Send this email to the customer if there’s proof that they already paid the pro.
PNP: Customer won't pay - cx: Send this email to the customer if they let us know they aren’t willing to pay the pro.
PNP: Customer will/has paid - pro: Send this email to pro if the customer is willing to pay or has already paid them.
PNP: Pro wants more help: Send this email to the pro if they let us know they want more help or think we haven’t done enough.
PNP: Customer doesn’t want help: Use if the customer tells us about a concern with their project, but doesn’t want our help.
PR: More info needed: Send this email to the pro when they’ve reported a T&S concern, but we need more info to investigate their concern further.
PR: Unresponsive - Follow up: Send this email to the pro when we’ve already asked for more info, but haven’t heard back.
PR: Thanks and sorry: Send this email to the pro when they’ve reported a negative experience, and there’s no further follow up or action needed.
PR: Safety concerns - pro: Send this email to the pro when they’ve reported safety concerns with a customer.
PR: Review dispute: Send this email to the pro when they’ve reported a negative experience, but we also need to address a review dispute request.
PR- Refund: Send this email to the pro when they’ve reported a negative experience, and we’re issuing a refund for the lead.
PR: Self reports - Set expectations: Send this email to the pro if they’ve reported a customer’s concerns with a project, but the customer hasn’t reported the project themselves.
PR: Self-Reports - Flag and warn: Send this email to the pro if they’ve reported a concern, but you’ve found behavior issues that warrant coaching.
**Use the content request form to request an update or submit questions/concerns**

What
​​(return to index)
Pro Abuse Investigation (PAI) is a queue where pro accounts are flagged for manual review if they show signals matching previously identified deceptive accounts. The Trust and Safety team will evaluate if the flagged account exhibits any deceptive behavior and should be removed from our platform. 
Why
​​​​(return to index)
Pros who engage in deceptive practices contribute to negative experiences for other users. Deceptive practices violate our Terms of Use and ultimately decreases user trust inThumbtack, leading to a higher churn rate and loss of revenue. 
When
​​(return to index)
A WT is created anytime a new pro account is linked to a previously identified deceptive account by either: 
Device ID, or

articles.concepts: non-discrimination policy, prohibited discrimination, protected classes, fair treatment, violations
articles.fullText:
Non-Discrimination

Non-Discrimination (incidents)
(Knowledge index)
INDEX
WHAT
WHY
WHEN
HOW
Steps
Process overview
Confirm a violation
Justified customer requests
Job-relevant gender preference
Support minority-owned businesses
Wedding officiant
Language barriers
Determine severity
Take action
In-product reports
Profile review
Tracker
Details
External reports
Talking points
Emails
What
(return to Index) 
Thumbtack’s Non-Discrimination Policy prohibits discrimination against users based on age, disability, gender identity, marital status, medical condition, national origin, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, or other improper basis.
Content posted on Thumbtack or improper behavior related to the characteristics above is not allowed. Reports of discrimination are sent to Trust and Safety so we can review them further. We categorize these reports into six types: 
Expressed preference: User makes an inappropriate request to include or exclude a protected class.
Passing comments/generalizations: Stereotypes or generally prejudiced comments made about a protected class.
Vulgarity, slurs, name-calling, insults: Insults, derogatory language, and unprofessional or hateful communication based on a protected class.
Offered or charged different price: Changing the price a business offers or customer requests to pay based on a protected class.
Refused to hire/work: A user states they won’t work with a certain protected class.
Other: Typically vague reports, or interactions that don’t fit into any other category. 

Why
(return to Index)
Thumbtack values people and their equal and equitable treatment. We want everyone—regardless of race, religion, gender, age, sexual orientation, etc.—to feel safe using our platform.
Discrimination of any form is prohibited and addressed. This includes ensuring customers and pros have equal opportunities to hire or be hired for projects.
When
(return to Index)
Typically, discrimination is routed to the Discrimination queue, though concerns of discrimination may occur during any incident. If you encounter a potential issue through a case or incident, tag @non-discriminationteam in #askaspecialist_ts for assistance.
How
(return to Index)
    Steps
    (return to Index)
PROCESS OVERVIEW
(return to Index)
Review the initial case details.
Depending on the nature of the report and required action or follow-up, you may determine to communicate anonymously by excluding your name and scheduling link.
Respond to the reporting party to ask for additional info and documentation if more specifics are needed to fully understand what’s happened.
If the reporting party indicates they would feel more comfortable sharing details directly over the phone, be sure to share your scheduling link.
Review the documentation to determine if the interaction violates our policy.
Once you’ve confirmed a violation, determine the severity.
Consider factors such as:
Type of discrimination.
Undocumented vs. documented.
User to Thumbtack vs. user to user.
Unintentional vs. intentional violations.
Determine the appropriate action.
If there’s a project concern also involved, address those concerns first.
If we’ll be removing the user, move forward with this action and look into assisting the customer through the Guarantee.
Take account action.
No action.
Notify user of policy.
Coach and warn.
Remove.
Close the incident.
CONFIRM A VIOLATION
(return to Index)
When we receive reports of violations, we still need to review them to confirm whether the interaction is a true violation of our policy.
*Trigger warning: examples used throughout this article contain real user-generated language that is discriminatory*

VIOLATION
NON-VIOLATION
Expressed preference

Pro seeks to filter leads.
Ex. “Every Asian person I work for gives me a problem. Please don’t send me these leads anymore."
The customer doesn’t want to work with a protected class.
Ex. “Dependable non-chicanos preferred”.
Reasonable/justified customer request
Ex. “My child is more comfortable with a female tutor.”
Ex. “I need a Nigerian makeup artist for my traditional Nigerian wedding.”
Job-relevant gender preference.
Ex. “I specialize in helping women get strong and fit.”
Support minority-owned businesses.
Ex. “I'd like to support a local small black-owned business.”
Passing comments/generalization

Inappropriate or negative stereotypes
Ex. “All the illegal aliens from Mexico are flooding the work industry and undercutting prices.”
Assumptions or generalizations made about a person’s protected class.
Ex. “The cleaners looked like they’re from Mexico, and I wonder if they’re here legally.”
Ex. “That man is too old to be working. He needs to retire already.”
Comments promoting an “us vs. them” mindset.
Ex. “Learn English if you want to live in this country.”
Mentioning a protected class or characteristic without negative commentary.
Ex. “The man that showed up was black, which didn’t match the profile photo.”
When context affects the meaning and direction.
Ex. "The man that showed up was black, which didn’t match the profile photo.”
Vulgarity, slurs, name-calling

Insults based on protected class.
Ex. “He called us lesbian b****es and wished we would die.”
Ex. “It’s unnatural! You fairies are corrupting our society!”
Slurs/blocklisted words.
“So u leave me a 1 star because I tried to help u go f*** urself n***er.”
Not about a protected class. (race, gender, national origin, etc.)
Ex. “You right-wing pig.”
Not directed at someone.
Ex. “This is a real b****.”
Charged/offered different price

Increasing the price of a job due to a protected class.
Ex. “You Indian people always like to complain, so for you this will cost double.”
Offering to pay less due to a protected class.
Ex. “A Mexican shouldn’t earn that amount. I’ll pay half that.”
Requesting a different price based on experience or not a protected class.
Ex. “Do you have anyone in training or less-skilled laborers that would cost less?”
Charging more based on details of a job.
Ex. “Since you live so far out of the city, there will be an extra travel fee.” 
Refused to hire/work

Wedding vendor turns down same-sex wedding.
Ex. “I'm sorry but we do not photograph same-sex weddings."
User declines to work with another due to a protected class.
Ex. “Sorry I didn’t see your name. I don’t work with Hispanics.”
Pro’s profile explicitly excludes a protected class.
Ex. “ONLY women, absolutely NO MEN.”
Wedding officiant declines due to religious reasons.
Ex. “I’m sorry, I don’t officiate same-sex weddings.”
Ex. “I only officiate Christian weddings.”
Declines to service a location based on measurable safety concerns.
Ex. “Crime rate is too high, I won’t go here.”
Other

Vague reports.
Ex. “They were very racist to me.”
Language barrier
Ex. “They didn’t speak English so we weren’t able to clarify all that needed to be done.”

Note: An interaction may not violate our Non-Discrimination Policy, but still be a concern that needs to be addressed and actioned, such as quality issues or unprofessionalism.
Justified customer requests
(return to Index)
There are times when a customer request may seek a specific characteristic for their job. Some factors that make certain preferences reasonable: 
Safety related precautions (especially in categories working with children)
Child is more comfortable with a certain gender for their 1:1 lessons.
A woman home alone during the cleaning feels safer having a female cleaner.
Relevant and appropriate to the nature of the job they’re hiring for.
An all-women’s conference is looking to hire a female photographer.
Requesting black male vocalists to sing romantic ballads made famous by the great black male groups of the 70s.
Customer requests and preferences in choosing who to hire have less liability than a business’s preferences in choosing, so we want to be understanding of the customer’s position while still holding to the essence of our policy and values.  
Job-relevant gender preference
(return to Index)
Gender can be relevant to the nature of some service categories due to safety concerns or proper expertise, so we wouldn’t consider a gender preference request a violation. This applies to:
Boudoir Photography
Personal Training
Nutritionist
Yoga Instruction
Reflexology/Alternative healing
While we don’t consider these violations, these leads are not valid refunds because they were valid leads that matched their product preferences.
The guiding principle in these situations should always be their reason for the preference. If the pro’s reason isn’t one of the above, confirm the violation.
Note: These will often come through in-product reports and profile review, so review these for the appropriate follow-up.
Support minority-owned businesses
(return to Index)

Thumbtack stands behind under-represented minority-owned businesses and supports customers in their efforts to do this as well. However, the customer’s intent needs to be support and inclusion of an underrepresented minority group, not exclusion of another group.
When this happens, we don’t need to take any action on the customer. Pros who report this may be eligible for a courtesy refund if they don’t match the customer’s preference.
Wedding officiant
(return to Index)

One narrow exception is with wedding officiants, not other wedding vendors. Since religion is central to the job a wedding officiant is hired to perform, a wedding officiant may decline a wedding request for religious reasons. We won’t remove their account unless the officiant was rude or offensive in doing so. 
Do not refund the lead.
Explain our policy to the user so they’re aware of our expectations.
Language barriers
(return to Index)

When a user states they struggled to communicate with another user because of a language barrier, this wouldn't be flagged. Comments explaining that a language difference made it hard are relevant details to completing and hiring for a project. Evaluate the context to ensure their intent aligns.
DETERMINE SEVERITY
(return to Index)
Once you’ve confirmed a violation, you’ll determine how the details and context of the interaction will impact the severity of our actions. To do this, consider the discrimination type and other factors:

[Image: Screenshot 2023-03-06 at 9.54.30 AM.png]

Undocumented vs. documented
(return to Index)

If the interaction is undocumented, depending on the details, this can be harder to confirm so may lend itself to less severe actioning. It’s common for interactions to not be documented; however, if the user can be specific, we can still use their experience when determining action. If the details are extreme and seem truthful or likely, then we can still take more severe action without documentation.
If the interaction is documented, this builds the severity of our action. An interaction can be documented:
On Thumbtack (messenger, review/responses, request comments, etc.)
Recorded (video/audio recordings)
Screenshot (through text, email, offsite)
Verify the message came from the user’s contact information.
User to Thumbtack vs. user to user
(return to Index)

When something is said to Thumbtack about another user or group, users on the platform have not been exposed. Because of this, we should lean towards less severe actioning, such as educating users on our policy and expectations.
Any interaction directly between users means individuals on the platform were exposed. To evaluate further, consider the speaker and audience involved:
Action more severely if:
A user references a group the reporting user identifies as.
Action less severely if:
A user is referencing a group they self-identify as.
A user is referencing a group neither party identifies with.

Note: If a user says something discriminatory towards you directly follow the steps outlined here.
Unintentional vs. intentional violations
(return to Index)

There are times when users unintentionally violate our policy or discriminate due to a lack of context or education. While these are violations, this lack of intentional ill-will could speak to the opportunity for changed behavior by providing coaching to educate them for future situations.
A driver was hired for a wine tour and turned away a customer with a service dog. 
This is unintentional if the driver didn’t know that failure to accommodate a service animal was discrimination.
A customer requested a video chat consultation, and the pro declined working with them. Customer then revealed they’re deaf.
This is unintentional if the pro didn’t know the reason for their accommodation request was a protected class, so they weren't refusing due to their disability.

When a user purposefully acts against our policy, based on a protected class, that would be an intentional violation. Tone or politeness does not factor into intent. While someone may be cordial and professional when declining to work with a protected class, their intention is still to not work with that group of people, which is discrimination.
Part of evaluating intent, beyond determining if it was purposeful, is also evaluating the motivation behind their words or actions. It might be difficult to determine, so please consider the context:

CONSIDERATION
EXAMPLE
Was there a change in response after the user disclosed a protected characteristic?
Users are communicating and excitedly planning the details of their couples photography session. As soon as the user discloses they are a same-sex couple, the pro immediately responds “Oh we’re not available anymore, sorry.”
Are there other comments/microaggressions carrying a negative undertone?
A user refers to a black woman as “loud and angry” when they are simply stating what was upsetting about their project outcome. This feeds into the negative racial trope of the “angry black woman.”
What is the unspoken message behind what they actually said or did?
A woman asks for clarifications on a project, and the other user responds, “How about you get your husband on the line and I can explain to him?"
While the user may just want to try speaking with someone else to reach an understanding, this could also come from implicit bias or an assumption that women don’t understand stereotypically “masculine” work.
Does the user have a history of flags or reviews for similar concerns?
The user has a previous flag related to being made aware of our policy, and their comments all seem to consistently demean the same particular group of people.

When you understand the meaning behind a user’s words or actions, you can better determine if it was motivated by intentional ill will or negativity. When this is the case, the interaction can be classified as hateful. Hateful interactions warrant more severe actioning. 
TAKE ACTION
(return to Index)
Once we’ve confirmed whether an interaction is a violation and determined the factors that affect the severity of our actions, we can determine the appropriate action for the offending user:

[Image: Screenshot 2023-03-08 at 3.51.51 PM.png]


ACTION
CIRCUMSTANCES
No action
No account action is common for interactions that aren’t confirmed violations (can include when a user is unresponsive and their report isn’t detailed), accepted preferences, reasonably justified customer requests.
Policy Reminder
Reminders are common for undocumented reports, unresponsive reporting party, and borderline comments, which may not violate but are unnecessary and/or inappropriate. 
Warning
Warnings are common for interactions made with Thumbtack about another user, user to user when the speaker self-identifies with the group they’re referencing, user to user when the audience doesn’t identify with the group referenced and slang.
Removal
Removals are common for documented interactions that are intentional, user-to-user, hateful, and involve blocklisted words or slurs.

Once you’ve determined the appropriate action, follow these steps:
Review for existing project concerns to address first.
Thank the user for their report.
If you’re removing the reported user, you can notify the reporting party now.
Move forward with the Guarantee to address any project concerns.
If the situation was self-reported by the offending user, determine if a user was exposed and if it’s supportive to the user to notify them of our action. Typically, do this only if we’re removing the offending user.
Complete account action.
No action.
Consider flagging to monitor potential patterns of behavior. (Grammarly shortcode, \NDP: Unresponsive flag).
Policy reminder.
Email the reported user (Grammarly short code \NDP: Notify of policy).
Flag the reported user’s account.
Coach and warn.
Email the reported user (Grammarly short code \NDP: Coach and warn).
If the user responds negatively, complete a comprehensive review to look into further potential action.
Flag the reported user’s account.
Remove.
Disable and blocklist the reported user.
Email the reported user (Grammarly short code \NDP: Removed, won't reconsider).
Remove your scheduling link.
If the user responds with questions, it’s best practice to respond at least once.
Close the incident.
in-product reports
(return to Index)

Pro reports of discrimination often come to us through in-product reports (IPSR/IPR). Before closing your incident, you’ll need to complete any attached in-product refund work tickets (WT).
Select the case attached to your incident with the WT details.
Tip: This may not be the customer or pro primary case.
Scroll down to the WT details and click on the refund request link to open in Admin.

[Image: Screenshot 2023-02-08 at 3.15.06 PM.png]

Action the refund request.
Select Refund Decision based on your review of the incident.
Denied_pro_reason_incorrect
Approved_questionable_job
Approved_other
Leave your T&S case number in Admin Note.
Select “Skip Notification (MTS only).”
Do not mark this if you are working a job-relevant gender preference  issue, so the pro receives a follow-up email from Thumbtack.

[Image: rtaImage]

Return to the WT in Tack and update the Outcome to match our action on the refund request.
Rejected
Approved
Note: If you receive an error when closing your incident that there is a pending WT after already completing these steps, update the Status to “Assigned”.
Profile Review
 (return to Index)

Some pros will get flagged for discrimination on their profiles, either manually or through the usual profile review process. While the usual process will result in their removal from the platform, if the pro falls under job-relevant gender preference, we’ll reconsider their account if they agree to change the wording in their profile.
Action pro’s account.
If the pro was already removed, reactivate their account and service profile if needed.
Add an account hold and select User has general issues or needs coaching.
In the notes, leave a brief description and your case number.
Email the pro notifying them they need to update their profile (Grammarly \NDP: Profile concerns).
Once the pro responds that it’s been updated, review their service introduction.
If the pro’s new description still doesn’t meet our requirements, you may need to call out the specific language they’re using, which we don’t allow.
If the new description meets our requirements: 
Remove the account hold.
Email the pro with an update on their status and thank them for cooperating.

     Tracker
      (return to Index)
Discrimination decision tracker
Review this sheet for a history of actioning within our policy. You’ll find specific examples of comments/interactions, severity factors, and the corresponding action we took. 
Continue to add to this sheet as new situations come up.

     Details
       (return to Index)
EXTERNAL REPORTS
(return to Index) 
Users sometimes report conduct outside of and unrelated to Thumbtack altogether. This can include someone reporting a user for their social media pages/posts, personal websites, affiliations, behavior in a public venue, etc. Generally, we are limited in the actions we can take for external reports, so the bar for verifying these reports as the same user on our site should be very high.
Ways to verify:
If trying to verify social media accounts, look for similar details such as:
Profile photos
Job title
Location
Contact information
Any other related content
Matching links that are included on their Thumbtack account.

If verified, consider the severity level and the risk to Thumbtack and our values. If the severity is mid to high and the risk is especially concerning or relevant, the non-discrimination team should loop in our cross-functional partners in Legal and DEI to help determine the action we’re able to take.
   Talking points
   (return to Index)
Talking points guide for speaking with pros - discrimination
User was removed for discrimination:
We were recently notified of an interaction that violates our Non-Discrimination Policy. The documentation we received showed [BRIEFLY, NEUTRALLY DESCRIBE VIOLATION]. After completing a thorough review, we’ve found that our Non-Discrimination Policy has been violated.
Due to this violation, we have closed your Thumbtack account. We didn’t make this decision lightly and we won’t be reconsidering the action we’ve taken.
Response: I should be able to pick and choose who I work with. That’s not discrimination.
You have the freedom to choose jobs that best suit you. However, declining to work with customers based on their [CHOOSE WHAT APPLIES: age, disability, gender identity, marital status, medical condition, national origin, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, etc.] is against our Non-Discrimination Policy.
If you’d like to know more, I’d be happy to email you the link to our Non-Discrimination Policy, as well as our Terms of Use.

Warn user for discriminatory language:
I know this is an upsetting situation. However, we consider those kind of statements to be discriminatory, and we won’t allow it to continue. It’s important that all of Thumbtack’s users are treated respectfully.
We have a clear Non-Discrimination Policy, which I’m happy to share with you. If you ever feel discriminated against, please let us know so we can help.
We want you to succeed, but speaking that way about anyone isn’t something that Thumbtack tolerates. We encourage you to be as professional, respectful, and kind as possible on Thumbtack.

Response: My values and beliefs affect who I'm willing to work with.
We understand each and every person may have different beliefs and values. However, picking and choosing your customers based on [CHOOSE WHAT APPLIES: age, disability, gender identity, marital status, medical condition, national origin, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, etc.] is against our Non-Discrimination Policy.

Response: Now you’re discriminating against me!
I’m sorry you haven’t felt more supported. We have a very strict Non-Discrimination Policy which aligns with our company values and actions. Being selective with customers based on specific characteristics isn't allowed on Thumbtack. We want you to feel empowered to make decisions based on your own expertise and preferences – not on your beliefs about other people, based on who they are.

Responding to a report of discrimination:
I’m sorry to hear about your experience. We expect users on our site to adhere to our Terms of Use, including our Non-Discrimination Policy. We take these concerns seriously, and we don’t want anyone to feel discriminated against. I'd like to make sure we look into this further so we take the appropriate action. Do you have any documentation or additional specifics about the interaction you can provide?
   Emails
   (return to Index)
GRAMMARLY AND TACK
NDP: Thank user for report: Use to thank the reporting user and let them know that we’ll be taking appropriate action.
NDP: More info needed: Use to gather additional information or documentation from the reporting user.
NDP: Unresponsive follow-up: This is used to gather additional information or documentation from the reporting user, and we haven’t received a response to our previous email.
NDP: Notify of policy: Use when you’re notifying a user of our Non-Discrimination Policy.
NDP: Coach and warn: Use when you’re coaching and warning a user for violation of our Non-Discrimination Policy.
NDP: Removed, wont reconsider: Use when you’re removing a user for violating our Non-Discrimination Policy.
NDP: Wedding officiant declines: Use when a wedding officiant has turned down a job due to religious reasons.
NDP: Profile concerns: Use when a pro was removed or flagged for their profile but falls under job-relevant gender preference.
NDP: Unresponsive flag: Flag for reported user when the reporting user was unresponsive, or we don’t have details on the offense/violation.
NDP: Coach and warning flag: Flag for when we have coached the reported user on their violation.
NDP: Notify pro, customer removed: Use this to let the pro know that we removed the reported customer.
NDP: HIPAA stepping back (customer): Send this to the customer if the dispute involves a confidentiality agreement or is protected by HIPAA laws.
NDP: HIPAA stepping back (pro): Send this to the pro if the dispute involves a confidentiality agreement or is protected by HIPAA laws.
NDP: Location discrimination: Use this macro to coach a user on location-based discrimination concerns.
NDP: Gender preference - Coach: Use this to coach a user for discrimination based on gender preference.
NDP: Professionalism warning: Use this to warn a user about their professionalism while interacting with other users.
NDP:  pro removed, Notify customer: Use this to inform a customer that the pro they reported has been removed.
NDP: Safety Concerns: Use this when the user has reported safety concerns but violated the Non-discrimination policy while doing so.
NDP: Towards TT Agents: Use this when a use has been discriminatory towards a TT support user.
GRAMMARLY ONLY
NDP: Link: Use this Grammarly snippet when you need to share the Non-discrimination policy.
NDP: Valid Lead: Use this to let the pro know that the lead they reported is valid.
NDP: Unresponsive flag: Flag for reported user when the reporting user was unresponsive or we don’t have details on the offense/violation.
NDP: Coach and warning flag: Flag for when we have coached the reported user on their violation.
NDP: Deletion log: Use for the deletion logs of a user we’ve removed for violating the Non-discrimination Policy.
